writer_rules: Use only the town and the street names given; never name a real town, city, county, state, agency, utility or company. Departments are named generically (the town clerk, the building department, public works). Emergencies are never handled on this line: the caller is told to hang up and dial 911.

scenarios.label: Permit question
scenarios.brief: The caller asks whether they need a permit for a home project (a deck, a fence, a shed, replacing a water heater) and how to apply. The clerk explains the steps and the fee in rough terms and how long a review takes.

scenarios.label: Property tax bill
scenarios.brief: The caller has a question about a property tax bill: the due date, a late notice, paying in installments, or a change after a reassessment. The clerk explains and says how to pay.

scenarios.label: Records request
scenarios.brief: The caller wants a certified copy of a birth or marriage certificate. The clerk asks who it is for, explains what ID is needed and the fee in rough terms, and how to pick it up or get it by mail.

scenarios.label: Recreation sign-up
scenarios.brief: The caller asks about signing a child up for a summer program or a class. The clerk explains the dates, the age range, the fee in rough terms and how to register.

scenarios.label: Missed trash pickup
scenarios.brief: The caller's trash or recycling was not picked up, or they want a bulk item collected. The dispatcher takes the street, explains the schedule and says when a truck will come back by.

scenarios.label: Pothole or streetlight report
scenarios.brief: The caller reports a pothole, a streetlight that is out, or a fallen branch on one of the streets named under Places. The dispatcher takes the location and a callback number and says when a crew can look at it.

scenarios.label: Water bill
scenarios.brief: The caller's water and sewer bill is much higher than usual. The clerk explains how the reading works, suggests checking for a running toilet or a leak, and offers to schedule a meter re-read.

scenarios.label: Recording request: copy
scenarios.brief: After the recording notice, the caller asks why calls are recorded, who can hear them, and how to get a copy of their recording. The clerk explains plainly and takes the request.

scenarios.label: Recording request: deletion
scenarios.brief: The caller is uncomfortable that the call is recorded and asks for the recording to be deleted. The clerk explains that town records follow retention rules, notes the request for the records officer, promises nothing they cannot do, and asks whether the caller still needs help.

scenarios.label: Hang-up on hold
scenarios.brief: The caller starts asking about a bill, the clerk asks them to hold while they find the right person, and the caller hangs up after waiting, saying they'll come in person instead.

scenarios.label: Screened robocall
scenarios.brief: An automated prerecorded pitch calls the town hall, offering a generic office supply deal that names no company. The clerk answers; the call is cut off by the line's screening announcement.

scenarios.label: Wrong number
scenarios.brief: The caller meant to reach someone else (the person named under People, or a kind of business, never a named one). The dispatcher says it's the wrong number, and the call ends quickly.

scenarios.label: After hours
scenarios.brief: The call comes in after the offices have closed and reaches the public works on-call dispatcher. The caller reports something that can't wait until morning (water bubbling up in the road, a tree across a street named under Places). The dispatcher takes the location and a callback number and sends the on-call crew.

scenarios.label: Voicemail
scenarios.brief: No one picks up. The first business turn is the clerk's office recorded voicemail greeting. The caller leaves a message with their name, the question and a callback number.
